Sugar Found In Meteorites May Have Helped Secure Its Own Survival On Early Earth

Sugar molecules found in meteorites may have helped create conditions that protected them from breaking down on early Earth, according to new research. The finding offers a possible explanation for how ribose, a fragile sugar that forms part of RNA, could have survived in environments where the chemistry of life was beginning to develop.

The study examines how ribose interacted with borate minerals and suggests that the relationship worked in both directions. Borate could protect ribose from chemical breakdown, while ribose could help keep borate dissolved in water.

Recreating The Chemistry Of Early Life

Scientists studying the origins of life often investigate how water, minerals and carbon-containing molecules could have interacted in Earth’s early environments. These mixtures may have existed in oceans, lakes or hot springs.

Changing temperatures, flowing water, mineral surfaces and evaporation could have driven increasingly complex chemical reactions. However, laboratory experiments often rely on purified chemicals and controlled conditions, which can leave out interactions found in natural environments.

RNA is an important focus of this research because it stores and uses genetic information in modern organisms. Scientists also think RNA may have played a role in the origin and early evolution of life.

However, RNA does not form easily. Its molecular backbone contains ribose, a fragile sugar that can break down when heated.

Boron Could Protect Fragile Ribose

One factor that can protect ribose is boron. In the form of borate, which contains boron, oxygen and hydrogen, the element can bind to ribose and help prevent it from breaking down.

Researchers examined this process using real minerals rather than only purified ingredients. They included borate crusts from Puga, a field of hot springs in India’s Himalayas.

The waters at Puga contain high concentrations of boron. Borate salt crusts can form there because minerals containing boron often dissolve poorly in water and instead precipitate into crystals.

That process leaves less dissolved boron available for chemical reactions. Therefore, researchers asked whether high concentrations of dissolved boron could realistically have existed in environments where life emerged.

Ribose May Have Helped Keep Boron Dissolved

The new study suggests that ribose itself may have helped solve this problem.

Researchers found that ribose helps borate minerals dissolve and inhibits the formation of solid grains. As a result, more boron can remain dissolved in water and stay available for chemical reactions.

The findings point to a two-way relationship. Borate can protect ribose from breaking down, while ribose can help keep borate dissolved.

This interaction could have affected the chemistry of early Earth, particularly in environments where carbon-containing molecules accumulated in water.

Meteorites Delivered Carbon Molecules

About four billion years ago, Earth looked very different from the planet today. The atmosphere contained little oxygen, while volcanic activity was widespread.

The young Earth was also subjected to heavy meteorite bombardment. These meteorites delivered water and carbon-containing molecules from space.

Researchers estimate that around a million tonnes of carbon could have arrived each year during this early period. The Murchison meteorite, which fell in Victoria in 1969, provides evidence of the types of molecules that may have reached Earth.

Scientists have identified ribose and other sugars among the meteorite’s contents. Without microbes to consume them, carbon-containing molecules could have accumulated where their supply exceeded chemical breakdown.

Evaporation in shallow lakes and pools, for example, could have concentrated organic molecules from space into chemically rich mixtures.

Primordial Chemistry May Have Shaped Minerals

Much origin-of-life research focuses on how minerals helped make the chemistry of early Earth more complex. The new study also considers the reverse process: how carbon-containing molecules may have changed the minerals around them.

Some boron that would otherwise have formed mineral crusts and become buried could instead have remained dissolved in primordial lakes and other waters.

Ribose was probably relatively rare, but other molecules, including ethylene glycol and glycerol, can also bind borate. Researchers say their effects on natural mineral deposits require further testing.

Other common components of Earth’s rocks, including silica and calcium, also interact with carbon-containing molecules. Therefore, primordial chemical mixtures may have influenced how some minerals and rocks formed.

Living organisms now influence geology through processes such as biomineralisation, which produces shells and coral skeletons. The research proposes that non-living carbon molecules may have influenced mineral formation even before life emerged.

Whether these interactions reshaped entire landscapes remains uncertain. However, studying them could help scientists refine theories about the origins of life and explore how similar processes might occur on other worlds.
